nodes.name: Soul
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: classic soul peaks in the mid-1960s, then keeps a steady presence, with a lift during the late-1990s neo-soul wave. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Gospel fervor meets rhythm and blues. The emotional and vocal foundation that funk, disco, and house all draw from.

nodes.name: Funk
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: 1970s peak, then a continuing scene and sample source, with a mid-2010s pop-funk moment. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Rhythm promoted to lead instrument: syncopated basslines and the one. James Brown's blueprint runs underneath electro, techno, and house.

nodes.name: Disco
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: the late-1970s boom and backlash, then repeated comebacks — the early-2000s French touch and nu-disco wave, the 2013 retro-disco moment, and the 2020 disco-pop revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Four-on-the-floor dance music born in New York's Black, Latino, and gay clubs. Its DJ culture and 12-inch single are the operating system of all later dance music.

nodes.name: Hip-hop
nodes.description: Bronx block-party culture built on breakbeats and turntables. Its electro branch loops straight into Detroit.

nodes.name: Krautrock
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: the original German movement, then rediscoveries through 1990s post-rock and late-2000s reissues and neo-kraut bands. Golden age means creative peak within this scene, not mainstream dominance.
nodes.description: West German experimental rock — motorik repetition and early synthesizers. The laboratory Kraftwerk emerged from.

nodes.name: Synth-pop
nodes.description: Pop songs built entirely from synthesizers, normalized by Kraftwerk and British new wave. Beloved on Detroit radio in the early 80s.

nodes.name: Italo disco
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: 1980s commercial peak, then a 2000s revival through electroclash and new Italo-inspired labels. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Disco rebuilt in Italy with drum machines and arpeggiated synths after the US backlash. Heavily imported by Chicago and Detroit DJs.

nodes.name: Hi-NRG
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original club and commercial peak, followed by continuing specialist scenes. Related styles have their own histories.
nodes.description: Fast, sequencer-driven post-disco descended from Moroder's productions. Proof that machines alone could carry a dancefloor.

nodes.name: Electro
nodes.description: Hip-hop's robotic cousin: TR-808 patterns and vocoders, crystallized by 'Planet Rock'. Cybotron made it Detroit's native language.

nodes.name: Chicago house
nodes.description: Disco stripped to the drum machine and rebuilt in Chicago clubs — named after the Warehouse. The first genre authored by DJs for DJs.

nodes.name: Garage house
nodes.description: The soulful, gospel-leaning New York strain of house, named after Larry Levan's Paradise Garage.

nodes.name: Deep house
nodes.description: House slowed and softened with jazz chords and soul vocals, defined by Larry Heard's 'Can You Feel It'.

nodes.name: Acid house
nodes.description: The squelch of a misused Roland TB-303, discovered by Phuture. Detonated UK youth culture in 1988.

nodes.name: Detroit techno
nodes.description: The Belleville Three fused funk, electro, and European synth music into futurist machine soul. Named by Juan Atkins; the trunk of the entire techno tree.

nodes.name: Minimal techno
nodes.description: Techno reduced to its skeleton — one idea, slowly mutated. Pioneered by Robert Hood and Richie Hawtin out of Detroit's second wave.

nodes.name: Dub techno
nodes.description: Berlin's Basic Channel ran Detroit techno through dub reggae's echo chambers: chords dissolved into fog.

nodes.name: Trance
nodes.description: German strain of techno and acid house stretched into long hypnotic builds, born around Frankfurt.

nodes.name: Gabber
nodes.description: Rotterdam's answer to Detroit: techno pushed past 160 BPM with distorted kicks.

nodes.name: Breakbeat hardcore
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original UK rave peak, then a specialist scene and a 2010s rave-revival comeback. Not an extinction date.
nodes.description: UK rave's first mutation: acid house energy welded to sped-up hip-hop breakbeats. The big bang of the UK continuum.

nodes.name: Jungle
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original 1990s UK breakthrough, a long underground stretch, then a clear late-2010s revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Hardcore's breakbeats chopped into polyrhythms over reggae basslines — Black British sound-system culture at rave tempo.

nodes.name: Drum and bass
nodes.description: Jungle refined into a sleeker, technoid form — rolling breaks at 170+ BPM.

nodes.name: UK garage
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: late-1990s UK commercial peak, a quieter stretch, then a gradual 2010s–2020s revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: US garage house pitched up and swung for London, absorbing jungle's bass culture into 2-step.

nodes.name: Dubstep
nodes.description: UK garage hollowed out in Croydon: half-tempo sway, sub-bass pressure, dub space.

nodes.name: Kraftwerk
nodes.description: Düsseldorf's man-machines. 'Trans-Europe Express' and 'Computer World' are cited by Juan Atkins and Afrika Bambaataa alike as the source code.

nodes.name: Giorgio Moroder
nodes.description: Munich producer whose fully sequenced 'I Feel Love' (1977) proved electronic dance music could be the future, not a gimmick.

nodes.name: Juan Atkins
nodes.description: The originator: coined 'techno', recorded as Cybotron and Model 500, founded Metroplex. One third of the Belleville Three.

nodes.name: Derrick May
nodes.description: The innovator of the Belleville Three. 'Strings of Life' gave techno its emotional ceiling; founded Transmat.

nodes.name: Kevin Saunderson
nodes.description: The elevator of the Belleville Three. Took techno to the pop charts with Inner City; founded KMS.

nodes.name: Belleville Three
nodes.description: Atkins, May, and Saunderson — high-school friends from Belleville, Michigan, who invented Detroit techno between mixtapes and Metroplex.

nodes.name: Cybotron
nodes.description: Juan Atkins and Rik Davis. 'Clear' (1983) is the hinge between electro and techno.

nodes.name: Frankie Knuckles
nodes.description: The Godfather of House. His edits and drum-machine experiments as Warehouse resident birthed the genre that took the club's name.

nodes.name: Ron Hardy
nodes.description: Music Box resident whose raw, manic sets made Chicago's wildest records — he broke 'Acid Tracks' from a cassette.

nodes.name: Larry Levan
nodes.description: Paradise Garage resident; his eclectic, emotional marathon sets defined garage house and modern DJ culture.

nodes.name: Phuture
nodes.description: DJ Pierre, Spanky, and Herb J. Twisting a TB-303's knobs past reason, they invented acid house with 'Acid Tracks'.

nodes.name: Jeff Mills
nodes.description: The Wizard. Co-founded Underground Resistance, then defined hard minimal techno on Axis and early Tresor.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit's masked, militant second-wave collective — techno as Black liberation politics, no major labels, no faces.

nodes.name: Richie Hawtin
nodes.description: Windsor's Plastikman, across the river from Detroit. Stripped acid and techno down to minimal's blueprint.

nodes.name: Carl Craig
nodes.description: Second-wave Detroit polymath, May's protégé — stretched techno toward jazz and orchestras on Planet E.

nodes.name: Goldie
nodes.description: Graffiti writer turned jungle auteur. 'Timeless' and his Metalheadz label took drum and bass to the world.

nodes.name: Metroplex
nodes.description: Juan Atkins' label — release M-001, Model 500's 'No UFO's', is techno's founding document.

nodes.name: Transmat
nodes.description: Derrick May's label. 'Strings of Life' and the Transmat seal: emotional futurism from Detroit.

nodes.name: KMS
nodes.description: Kevin Saunderson's label, bridge between Detroit techno and the global charts via Inner City.

nodes.name: Trax Records
nodes.description: Chicago's chaotic house factory — 'Acid Tracks', 'Your Love', and most of the genre's canon on recycled vinyl.

nodes.name: Tresor
nodes.description: Berlin club and label in a bank vault under Potsdamer Platz; the Detroit–Berlin axis made concrete after the Wall fell.

nodes.name: Detroit
nodes.description: Post-industrial Motor City. Assembly lines, WGPR radio, and The Electrifying Mojo set the conditions for techno.

nodes.name: Chicago
nodes.description: Where disco survived its backlash underground and mutated into house.

nodes.name: New York
nodes.description: Birthplace of disco DJ culture, hip-hop, and the Paradise Garage.

nodes.name: Düsseldorf
nodes.description: Rhineland industrial city; home of Kraftwerk's Kling Klang studio.

nodes.name: Berlin
nodes.description: Reunified city of empty vaults and power plants that adopted Detroit techno as its soundtrack.

nodes.name: London
nodes.description: Sound-system capital where acid house became rave, and rave became a 30-year continuum.

nodes.name: I Feel Love
nodes.description: Donna Summer, produced by Giorgio Moroder — the first all-sequencer dance hit. Eno: 'This is the sound of the future.'

nodes.name: Clear
nodes.description: Cybotron's electro landmark: the exact midpoint between 'Planet Rock' and techno.

nodes.name: No UFO's
nodes.description: Model 500 (Juan Atkins), Metroplex M-001. Widely cited as the first techno record.

nodes.name: Strings of Life
nodes.description: Rhythim Is Rhythim (Derrick May). Piano stabs and strings with no bassline — techno's emotional anthem.

nodes.name: Acid Tracks
nodes.description: Phuture on Trax. Twelve minutes of TB-303 squelch that named and defined acid house.

nodes.name: Your Love
nodes.description: Frankie Knuckles and Jamie Principle — Chicago house's tenderest anthem.

nodes.name: The Warehouse
nodes.description: Frankie Knuckles' Chicago club. Members-only, mostly Black and gay — 'house music' is literally its record-store shorthand.

nodes.name: Paradise Garage
nodes.description: Larry Levan's New York church of sound; 'garage' as a genre is its namesake.

nodes.name: Music Institute
nodes.description: Detroit's short-lived, juice-bar-only techno club — the home floor of the first and second waves.

nodes.name: Second Summer of Love
nodes.description: Acid house hits Britain: warehouse parties, orbital raves, and a moral panic that forged UK dance culture.
